content: A palindrome is a sequence of characters, such as a word, phrase, number, or other arrangement, that reads the same forward and backward. Adjustments to punctuation and spacing are typically allowed. Writing literature in the form of palindromes is an example of constrained writing. The term palindrome originates from the Greek roots palin (meaning back) and dromos (meaning way or direction). It was coined by the English writer Ben Jonson in the 1600s. In Greek, the phenomenon is described as karkinike epigrafe (meaning crab inscription) or simply karkinikeoi (meaning crabs), referencing the backward movement of crabs, akin to an inscription that can be read in reverse. One of the most famous palindromes is the Latin word square Sator Arepo Tenet Opera Rotas, discovered as graffiti in Herculaneum, which was buried by volcanic ash. This palindrome is notable because it reproduces itself when letters are rearranged into a word square, allowing it to be read in multiple directions: horizontally, vertically, and diagonally. Some sources translate it as The sower Arepo holds the wheels at work, but the meaning is debated, as the word Arepo is otherwise unknown. It may have been a coded Christian symbol, with TENET forming a cross. Another example is a Hebrew palindrome by Ibn Ezra, which translates to We explained the glutton who is in the honey was burned and incinerated. This refers to a halachic question about whether a fly landing in honey renders the honey non-kosher. Similarly, the Latin palindrome In girum imus nocte et consumimur igni translates to We go wandering at night and are consumed by fire, and is thought to describe the behavior of moths. This palindrome likely originates from medieval times rather than antiquity. Byzantine Greeks often inscribed the palindrome Wash my sins, not only my face on baptismal fonts. Examples of such inscriptions can be found at St. Mary’s Church in Nottingham, the Basilica of St. Sophia in Constantinople, and other churches across Europe. In Sanskrit poetry, palindromes of remarkable complexity were explored. An example from the 8th-century epic poem Śiśupāla-vadha by Māgha is considered one of the most intricate palindromes ever created. It can be read forwards, backwards, upwards, and downwards, demonstrating extraordinary symmetry. In English, the most familiar palindromes are character-based, such as civic, level, rotor, and racecar. Palindromic phrases and sentences also exist, such as Was it a rat I saw? and Step on no pets. Punctuation, capitalization, and spacing are often ignored in these cases. Some individuals have palindromic names, either given at birth or adopted later, such as actor Robert Trebor. Palindromes can also be word-based rather than letter-based. Examples include Fall leaves after leaves fall and First Ladies rule the State and state the rule: ladies first. Some palindromes combine both character and word symmetry, such as Level, madam, level. In poetry, palindromes can take the form of entire lines. For instance, James A. Lindon’s poem Doppelganger is a line-by-line palindrome. Similarly, the dialogue Crab Canon in Douglas Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach mirrors lines spoken by characters in reverse order. In molecular biology, palindromic DNA sequences are recognized by restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at specific sites. These sequences are palindromic because their complementary strands read the same backward as forward. For example, the sequence ACCTAGGT is palindromic because its reverse complement is TGGATCCA. Palindromic DNA can form hairpin structures and is often found in bacterial chromosomes and other genetic elements. On the Y chromosome, palindromic structures allow self-repair by folding at the midpoint. In mathematics, palindromic numbers are those that read the same backward and forward, such as 58285. Palindromic primes are palindromic numbers that are also prime. Palindromic dates, such as February 20, 2002 (20-02-2002), are of interest to recreational mathematicians and numerologists. In music, palindromes appear in compositions such as crab canons, where one melody is reversed in time and pitch. Examples include Johann Sebastian Bach’s The Musical Offering and works by composers like Béla Bartók, George Crumb, and Anton Webern. Webern’s music often features horizontal and vertical symmetry, as seen in his Opus 21 Symphony and Opus 27 Piano Variations. In popular culture, palindromes are used in song lyrics and titles. For example, I Palindrome I by They Might Be Giants features palindromic lyrics, and Bob by Weird Al Yankovic consists of rhyming palindromes. Other examples include Andrew Bird’s album Noble Beast, which incorporates palindromic elements in its tracks. Acoustic palindromes, where recorded speech sounds the same when played backward, were discovered by composer John Oswald in 1974. For instance, the phrase I got spoken by William S. Burroughs retained its sound when reversed. The longest palindromic word in the Oxford English Dictionary is tattarrattat, coined by James Joyce in Ulysses to mimic the sound of a knock on the door. Other long palindromic words include detartrated and rotavator. In Finnish, the word saippuakivikauppias (soapstone vendor) is considered the longest palindromic word in everyday use. In genetics, palindromic motifs are common in DNA and proteins. These sequences often play roles in structural and functional aspects of biomolecules, though their exact significance in proteins remains unclear. In computational theory, the set of all palindromes in a given alphabet is context-free but not regular, meaning it cannot be reliably tested by a finite-memory computer. Finally, semordnilap is a term for words or phrases that spell different words or phrases backward. For example, stressed becomes desserts when reversed. These are also known as heteropalindromes or reversible anagrams and are useful in constructing palindromes.
